title: POC Weekly Caching Sync - Prefix/KV Cache Review
summary: Weekly POC sync to review prefix and KV cache hit rate improvements, discuss prompt reuse/normalization strategies, and plan next tuning steps. We reviewed recent benchmark runs where hit rates improved after template canonicalization, discussed failure modes (user-specific tokens breaking prefix cache), agreed on normalization and TTL adjustments, and assigned actions: Maya to share updated config and scripts, Tom to run a 48-hour load test with new keys, Alex to provide cost/ops notes and security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (BrightLayer - ML), Priya Nair (BrightLayer - Eng Lead), Samir Rao (BrightLayer - Infra)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is the weekly POC caching sync. quick roll call?
[00:12] Tom: Tom here.
[00:14] Priya: Priya on.
[00:16] Samir: Samir as well.
[00:18] Maya: Maya, hi.
[00:20] Alex: Cool. Agenda — sync on the last 72 hour run, prefix/KV hit rates, discuss prompt reuse strategy and any infra blockers.

[01:05] Maya: Alright so quick summary from our side. we ran the canonicalization pass on the prompt templates, removed user-specific tokens from the prefix and introduced a short hash for the session-id so it doesn't vary the entire prefix. preliminary numbers look good: overall prefix hit rate went from 28% to about 46% on a sample trace of 150k reqs. kv cache hit rate is a bit lower — around 39% — because some payloads still have non-deterministic sections.

[02:10] Tom: wait, 46% prefix sounds great, where did the rest of the gain come from? we thought KV would be the main lever.

[02:20] Maya: yeah so prefix and KV are related. prefix caching saves the initial token computation and KV cache helps for repeated continuations. by normalizing the prefix we avoid cache fragmentation — previously tiny differences in CIDs and timestamps created unique keys. after normalization, more requests hit the same key. we also adjusted TTLs to 10 minutes for short-lived sessions and 24 hours for templates that are stable.

[03:05] Priya: can you explain the canonicalization step again, we want to be sure it won't leak PII or change semantics?

[03:14] Maya: absolutely — canonicalization is purely syntactic: we replace user identifiers with a fixed placeholder token and strip volatile fields like request-trace id. we also collapse whitespace and standardize datetime formats (ISO without timezone). semantics should remain the same because the model's prompt logic treats those fields as metadata. we documented rules in the script — will share link after the call.

[04:22] Samir: any code we should run on our side or is this all done upstream at Redwood?

[04:29] Alex: good question — we shipped two options: client-side normalization library (small JS/Python) and server-side canonicalization at the routing layer. for the POC we recommended client-side because it reduces load on your network and lets you control privacy. Maya will share the client libs.

[05:00] Tom: ok we'll try the client lib. one concern: some of our prompts include short-lived tokens (like a 6-char feature flag). don't want to break personalization.

[05:18] Maya: right — we recommend scoped placeholders: if the token is semantically required for personalization, keep it but move it to the tail of the prompt (not the prefix) so it doesn't fragment prefix cache. or we add a second-level key: base-prefix + personalization-suffix so KV can still apply for the base.

[06:12] Priya: what's the memory impact of raising TTLs? we're on a constrained dedicated pool.

[06:19] Maya: TTL increases linearly with unique keys kept in memory. we measured per-key overhead at ~1.2 KB for metadata + kv entries size depends on model step size; for your workload with 200k unique templates we estimate ~250MB extra. if you want we can provide a detailed memory model.

[07:05] Samir: that 250MB is okay, but how does it affect eviction? LRU or ARC?

[07:12] Maya: Redwood's runtime uses segmented LRU with hot/cold separation; we can tune the hot partition for pinned templates. for POC we increased hot partition to 30% which preserved high-frequency templates and improved hit rates.

[08:00] Tom: Maya earlier mentioned KV hit rate lagging prefix — what's the plan to boost KV hits?

[08:10] Maya: two levers: 1) align continuation tokens by making prompts produce more deterministic lengths (e.g., set a max tokens and pad deterministic suffix tokens), 2) group similar prompt families into same shard so KV entries are colocated. we adjusted batching to avoid partial KV writes. after those changes we saw KV hit rate rise modestly from 26% to 39%.

[09:05] Priya: are any of these changes likely to change the quality/regression stats? we track answer correctness and don't want regressions.

[09:18] Alex: great point — we ran the evaluation harness against your red-team prompt set. quality metrics (accuracy and relevant F1) were within 0.6% of baseline. the canonicalization didn't change semantics in our tests. we'll include the eval diff in the doc bundle.

[10:02] Tom: can you share the raw numbers? p50/p95 latency and cost delta?

[10:12] Maya: sure — for the sample run: overall p50 token latency on hosted with cache on hit was 190ms vs 320ms cold; p95 was 780ms vs 1.2s cold. token cost per request dropped ~14% when combining prefix and KV. note these numbers depend on batching and sequence length distribution.

[11:05] Samir: interesting. for our throughput target (200 req/s sustained) do you think the routing will keep up if more hits occur?

[11:15] Maya: routing is stateless and scales horizontally; more cache hits reduce GPU work so it actually eases pressure. we did a stress test with synthetic 250 rps and the caches reduced GPU utilization by ~22%.

[12:00] Priya: what are the failure modes? when cache misses spike, do we have graceful degradation?

[12:09] Alex: yes we have fallback policies: if a cache miss triggers high latency we can route to a lower-latency model variant or to a dedicated hot pool; also canary throttles and circuit-breakers. we'll demo the fallback policy in the technical deep dive.

[13:00] Tom: quick note: some of our requests include user-uploaded snippets that vary a lot; those are main source of fragmentation. any pattern suggestions?

[13:12] Maya: treat upload content as a separate input and either store as object reference (URI) or hash the content and pass only the hash in the prefix. you can then fetch content server-side for context window if needed. that avoids prefix fragmentation.

[14:05] Priya: does that create extra fetch latency?

[14:12] Maya: small overhead if object store is nearby, but usually cheaper than losing cache hit. you can also precompute embeddings or summaries and store them as stable keys.

[15:05] Tom: about prompt reuse strategy — we have many slightly different templates. is there a recommended canonical template taxonomy?

[15:18] Maya: yes: group templates by intent, canonicalize variable slots, and maintain a template registry with versioning. we recommend three layers: base intent -> template variant -> session personalization. base intent is what's cached. versioning lets you invalidate keys on updates.

[16:20] Alex: quick administrative item — Maya will push the config and scripts to the shared folder. Tom, can you run the 48 hour test with the client normalization by next week?

[16:30] Tom: yes we can. Samir will help integrate the client lib into the edge service.

[17:00] Samir: one question on security — if we hash user content, what about compliance and KMS? do you store raw content?

[17:08] Alex: Redwood doesn't store raw customer data in hosted unless configured; for Dedicated you control KMS and retention. we can provide SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes — I'll attach. hashing is deterministic; if you need salted hashes for compliance we can support that.

[18:15] Priya: what about monitoring — do you surface cache hit telemetry per template?

[18:22] Maya: yes, Console has per-template hit rates, per-route token cost, and KV/prefix split. we can add an alert when hit rate drops below a threshold.

[19:05] Tom: can we get an export of the sample run trace? I'd like raw keys and anonymized prefixes to audit fragmentation causes.

[19:12] Maya: yes we'll provide an anonymized trace with keys replaced by deterministic placeholders.

[20:00] Alex: let's do a quick recap and next steps. we saw prefix hit improvement to ~46% after canonicalization; KV improved to ~39% after batching and shard tuning. quality regression negligible. actions: Maya share configs and script, Tom run 48h load, Alex send security docs and estimated cost delta.

[21:10] Priya: timeline looks good. one ask — can we schedule deep dive w/ infra for fallback policies? week of May 18 works.

[21:22] Alex: noted. we'll schedule that.

[22:00] Tom: one last quick question — any tips for prompt designers to maximize reuse?

[22:08] Maya: yes: prefer slots over inline tokens, avoid embedding unique ids in the prefix, normalize whitespace and date formats, and use controlled vocab for intent labels. we'll add a short best-practices doc.

[23:00] Alex: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the bundle (configs, eval diffs, trace) and action items.

[23:10] Meeting end.
